en: Through a six-month hardship,
Guard your honor, and set out,
Go to learn his inner secret,
Without tiring, without faltering,
Do not cast away your honor in shame,
Go to learn the warrior’s secret,
Go to the one who came beneath the standard,
One man fit to face a thousand,
He has a wrestler’s strength and a lion’s courage,
When he meets a foe, he makes the soul recoil,
My dark lord, you possess it all,
A swift horse unsurpassed in horsemanship,
Your name is known throughout the world,
Behold your formidable fury,
When many enemies stood all around,
You have a champion plainly in sight.
You have the force to stir turmoil to its roots,
Even your wisest one has a flaw,
When he turns to disorder among the Burut,
You have one who levels a spear like wheat,
When battle joins, you have one who bathes them in blood,
Without losing the way in darkness,
You have one who ties them at the watch-post and shoots,
You have one who plunges into blood and fury,
You have one who turns back those who flee.
From the burden laid upon Ala-Too,
Putting out the fire they kindled,
Driving their lives from their bodies,
Without letting his back touch the ground,
Without mounting him on some poor nag,
Without letting his people pasture in the mountains,
Without letting them sow any crops,
Without letting them tether even two mares,
Let us give them no time to gather their senses,
Let us give them no time to rest.
Without letting them live by their own will,
Without letting them linger even two days,
Without letting a single one settle by himself,
Let us bind their bands of thirty,
Let us lay their bands of thirty low,
Their heroes and their lions,
Let us spill the blood of their chiefs,
Their unbridled ones who know no master,
Let us quench their breath in the water.
This Kurman seems to be Külchoro,
Let us dig out the roots of the slaves.
If strife rises from his ashes.
Let us scatter their blood like seed,
Let us strike at their people,
[Uncertain: They have made that land their camp,]
Saying, ‘If you wish, a detachment of a thousand,’
Let us overrun Tobochokon,
[Uncertain: Let us set the rolling host aflame,]
We shall deal with their people as we see fit,
We shall plunder without leaving a soul and then rest.
[Uncertain: Let us despoil those who are broken,]
If the accursed enemy breaks apart,
Let us make it one realm,
Among the people who raised their royal camp,
After taking counsel, we shall appoint a champion,
Of the Burut who poses as a hero,
One who would plunder everything,
Making a khan from among the Kalmyks,
Laying low whoever opposes us,
Let us make their land a fortress,
Rather than leave even one among the Burut,
[Uncertain: Let us take the land and learn their intent.]
Learn the disposition they have,
Learn their hidden ways from their backs.
Their brave men and their marksmen,
Learn them again and again.
Putting their very lives into it,
Without revealing their inner secret,
They learn one another’s intent beforehand.
How many roads there are, how many cliffs,
The bounds of their barriers,
The mountain passes girded with barriers,
The places they have bound fast,
Their great lords and their khans,
By name—
[Uncertain: Distinguish what people they are called,]
Of the souls accustomed to that land,
Observe them carefully from afar.
Taking measure of how long the road is,
Come and range across this ground.
Go out scouting and survey the land,
Keep watch and reconnoiter the country,
Let us see which way there is movement.
Take the measure of the army,
Stand ready again, comrades,
Heroes ready for the hunt,
Enter the battle without fleeing,
Fulfil the duty owed to the people,
Go today for the people of Beijing,
For the people and lives of the forty khans,
For all of this,
For the hero Khan Chyngteñir,
Who would die as a sacrifice,
If you go, do not stay behind—truth or falsehood,
The mortal who was born has seen it.
Behind him he has a splendid swift one,
He has a champion complete in every way.
He stayed watching this closely,
From him came my seven forefathers,
The common Kyrgyz move in an uproar,
They saw the full extent of it all.
Having seen it, make this known,
Its sovereign was wrathful,
If so, break the roadward side,
He goes on, supporting and driving them,
He had remained after seeing many things.
They are numerous, but have no sense,
They are a thriving Chinese people,
If you sit and look upon their multitude,
They are black vermin beyond counting,
Unable to master even this small people,
Your driving them has brought disgrace.
Short of wit and without honor,
With no brave man to inspire awe,
With little pride and without honor,
Their heads are dark, their antlers forked,
These seem to be a hostile people to me.
Without courage and without honor,
What sort of great creature has emerged?
Kakan-chyn, khan of forty in battle,
This Beijing upon which light has fallen,
Owes a debt of words to our father,
Striking Aidarot against the people,
There is our father's grievance in it.
My Kaldais, my commanders,
A pearl-stone fit to wear as a necklace,
My warriors who stand dressed for battle,
My marksman reared for the letter's summons,
My hero who was left childless,
I joined what had not been joined,
Having seen much, both great and evil,
I asked the noblewomen.
After asking, I myself,
Burned and baked until I became an ember,
I mourned what had come for its sake.
I shall stand towering like a giant,
I waited and asked for their chief,
Neither eating food nor taking a meal,
I am wounded as though struck by a bullet,
My age has been overturned,
Thinking, I longed for many things.
In the fortress-gardens of Beijing,
In the time of my forefather, the radiant man,
Many wondrous decrees are written,
When I look upon the many decrees,
Dwelling in Alabotu,
A man who yielded to no one in combat!
Never sated in pursuing his plea,
When he drove them in the darkness,
He ranged abroad with the bearing of a leopard,
A poplar that grew among the mountain rocks,
Raging, he shook them and cut off heads,
The great man of Ak-Kainak,
The renowned Manas was born,
What remained of Aloötür Kakan,
The wondrous child who would raise his head.
He had finished his speech as well,
He had evidently set Beijing in order.
No soul could withstand his wrath,
Despairing even of their own lives,
Kakan’s people fell into turmoil.
The wise men assembled,
Learned men and heroes,
Despairing of life and soul,
Of Beijing in the land of the Chinese,
Men formidable in speech,
Shamans who could cast things into fire,
Singers accomplished in every device,
They became subdued and abject,
The stalwarts who could find a stratagem,
The strongest among the strong,
All kinds of men who could devise a way,
All of them became afraid.
Six generations under one battle cry,
Those descended from separate forefathers,
Three generations of Kyrgyz had slaughtered them.
To this Kakan who had settled here,
If we consider what those versed in lore say,
They came after making entreaties,
One cauldron for every household hearth,
They gave it, saying, “Make your living.”
Unable to endure his wrath,
The medicine called Közün struck,
And Kakan's people remained there.
The punishment and affliction of Qin Shi,
He had handed him over into powerful hands.
His wrath had been fierce,
For what these Kyrgyz had done,
Against Kakan of the forty Chinese tribes,
I am Börök of Beijing,
Of the great people of the forty Chinese tribes,
They had challenged his rule.
Upon the guilty men, by God,
A deed that was not forgotten had occurred,
Those supporters said to have fought,
Had formed countless hosts.
Their warriors had been like steel,
The blood of those who contended was spilled.
The solitary died, living souls died,
Soulless livestock died,
They committed an immense deed,
You did not fear the men,
Digging out their lives, you laid them straight,
You committed an unforgettable deed.
Cutting down those men,
He cut down the heroes and uprooted them,
What these Kyrgyz intend to do,
Will not be forgotten even when broken apart.
They are no people who wander idly,
Their temper is keen, with poison-like force,
These pressing Kyrgyz are no ordinary people.
I received news from the Kyrgyz,
From the Kyrgyz Khan Beken arose,
His spirit surging from his valor,
The thoroughbred he rode was itself heroic,
No land could hold them firmly,
There are no people like these in what they do,
That great one, they say, was a Kyrgyz,
When anger spoke, do not strike and break,
He was born, they say, among the Kyrgyz,
When he thrust like a ball, he took the prize,
By night he broke through and made a road,
Without delay he attacked the people,
One of understanding, they say, from the Kyrgyz.
The champion went straight against him,
Of the many souls who faced him,
They saw a place from which none returned.
Before long, so many souls,
Sat there having perished.
When one looks, such was the calamity.
Thus, among the Kyrgyz who stood there,
Know that his strength had wearied,
He drove them on, striking at their ranks,
Toward Sarkaluu’s settlement,
Come on, striking through the raid,
Great Beijing, the mighty people, fell into disorder,
If you see the shepherd, look at his coat,
Its warriors were exceptional,
Every man had recovered,
The unruly villain who acknowledged no leader,
Returned again to his place,
His people mounted up and went to war,
The people of Beijing—True Heaven,
He has honor, and his venom is strong,
That army is dense as a mountain.
When his frenzy seizes him,
The eighteen thousand worlds,
He has the might to lay waste.
He becomes a scourge upon the people,
When his furious demon seizes him,
The eighteen thousand worlds,
